# SpecAgent completion and review — 11 October 2026

The missing test coverage, design notes, sandbox games, local simulator games and hosted practice
evaluation have been completed. This is **not a full acceptance pass**: only P02, P04 and P11 meet
their rounded score targets, and a deliberately idled P05 bidder incurred a timeout. The remaining
performance gaps and explicit requirement deviations are recorded below, not hidden by the successful
deals or by the team's historical leaderboard bests.

## Verification

Final source: **204 tests passed, 1 skipped**, `ruff check arena_kit tests` clean, `git diff --check`
clean. The skipped test is the separately opted-in hosted smoke test for NaiveAgent/LLMAgent
(`ARENA_TEST_URL`/`ARENA_TEST_KEY`); SpecAgent's requested hosted games actually ran, with the
configured OpenAI `gpt-6-astra` model and the user's explicit permission.

| Requirement | Regression coverage |
|---|---|
| R11.2, R11.8, R11.12 | `tests/test_spec_analyst.py`: grounded extraction, decimal/sign boundaries, dates, nonfinite numbers, inherited prose lock-in, tactic eligibility |
| R11.14–R11.15, R12.17 | `tests/test_spec_clock.py`, `tests/test_spec_analyst.py`: virtual clocks, measured rounds, short/zero waves, early close, writer budget/fallback |
| R12.4, R12.14 | `tests/test_spec_steps.py`: inherited revealed slopes, costly lever exclusion, first RFQ rival citation without model waiting |
| R13.1–R13.7 | `tests/test_spec_steps.py`: one-term menus, ranking, option order, one reopen, real two-package choices after guards, persistent/overriding revealed locks, EN/DE alternatives, no identical resend |
| R13.9, R13.11, R13.15 | `tests/test_spec_claims_email.py`: index windows/rounding, rising-index eligibility, notice/ledger, case-only facts, exact volatility threshold, lint and real salutations |
| R13.16 | `tests/test_spec_clock.py`, `tests/test_spec_runner.py`: bounded rival wait, slow-POST polling, refused-accept refresh/retry, full local API games |
| Evaluation accuracy | `tests/test_spec_evaluate.py`: structured timeouts are detected even without timeout wording |

Existing pricing, coverage, sheet guard, close-rule and recorded-negotiation tests were rerun too.
Additional tests cover cost-neutral normal lead times and numeric equality of locked terms (`0` vs
`0.0`).

## Games and score table

D01 and D02 were played with the configured model: scores **0.786949** and **0.649788**, valid deals,
closed after **138.1** and **200.8** seconds from open. Evidence:
[D01](runs/spec-sandbox-d01/D01.json), [D02](runs/spec-sandbox-d02/D02.json).

All three clock-enabled local simulator cases also ended in valid deals: S01 **0.173886**, S02
**0.171836**, S03 **0.633926**. The final-source model repeat is in
[spec-sim-verified](runs/spec-sim-verified/summary.md). An initial simulator setup omitted the data
facts and produced contradicted IDs; the evaluator was corrected to supply the facts and the games
were repeated cleanly. Simulator scores test plumbing, not hosted negotiation quality.

The hosted model sweep is one complete ten-case run. The code-only column is a separate final-source
fallback benchmark, not a claim that model and non-model negotiations are interchangeable. Targets
are compared at three decimals because the requirements round historical raw scores.
The main model sweep preceded the last lead-time/volatility edits; the affected P05 negotiation was
retested with the lead-time fix, followed by a final-source model simulator repeat and a full
final-source code-only hosted sweep. Source fingerprints preserve these distinctions.

| Case | Target | Final code-only | Model sweep | Model seconds from open | Target met |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| P01 | 0.941 | 0.827854 | 0.631200 | 113.5 | No |
| P02 | 0.507 | 0.506721 | 0.506721 | 121.3 | Yes, rounded |
| P03 | 0.919 | 0.864105 | 0.864105 | 160.7 | No |
| P04 | 0.860 | 0.860445 | 0.860445 | 118.1 | Yes |
| P05 | 0.781 | 0.676181 | 0.521725 | 170.2 | No |
| P07 | 0.773 | 0.753477 | 0.714517 | 144.9 | No |
| P08 | 0.549 | 0.393752 | 0.332313 | 128.1 | No |
| P10 | 0.671 | 0.662905 | 0.647294 | 34.7 | No |
| P11 | 0.710 | 0.709896 | 0.709896 | 322.0 | Yes, rounded |
| P18 | 0.453 | 0.270425 | 0.319096 | 143.6 | No |

Model sweep mean: **0.610731 (61.07/100)**, versus target mean **0.716400 (71.64/100)**.
Final code-only sweep mean: **0.652576 (65.26/100)**; all ten valid deals, maximum closure time
185.6 seconds, but also one deliberately idled P05 bidder timeout. Fast cached supplier responses
in many repeated code-only games are not a guarantee of real-world latency.
The post-fix, model-backed P05 retest improved to **0.573210**, with 35-day lead time, but remains
below target. Its wall time includes pre-open profiling; closure from open was about 203 seconds.
It is a targeted retest, not a replacement ten-case mean.

Raw scores, threads, sessions, audit records, prompts/replies and source fingerprints:
[model sweep](runs/spec-practice-model/summary.md),
[final code-only sweep](runs/spec-practice-verified/summary.md),
[P05 retest](runs/spec-practice-p05-lead-fix/P05.json).
Earlier experiments are preserved in `runs/spec-practice-code`, `runs/spec-practice-fixed` and
`runs/spec-practice-final`; their intermediate regressions are not represented as successful fixes.

## Below-target investigation and fix outcomes

| Case | Evidence / cause | Fix or measured outcome |
|---|---|---|
| P01 | A lower-total-cost later-date package can need a higher unit price. The original generator rejected it. Model play also locked 30-day payment and a January date after the supplier priced an alternative; its cheaper alternative ID was refused by the arena. | Removed the unit-price ceiling while preserving total-cost/floor guards; enforced real choices after guards and persistent revealed locks. Code play improved from 0.759845 to 0.827854 and obtained April, but at EUR 136.85/30 days rather than historical EUR 135.20/60 days. Model play still missed. |
| P03 | Full coverage is correct. The first credible payment choices at the estimated convex-cost target were 30/45 days; the supplier chose 45 and held EUR 430.09. Historical target play achieved 90 days at EUR 432.29. | Fixed inherited prose slopes and actual-price locks. Repeated code/model games still scored 0.864105. The remaining gap is payment/anchor calibration, not a missing coverage or arithmetic fix. |
| P05 | Quote-PDF defaults carried unnecessary 28-day expedited delivery despite a 35-day need. Suppliers explicitly state that 28 days costs overtime. Dralveck countered at EUR 28, then walked after another low counter; Fuchsreiter became the remaining best deal. | Relax cost-neutral expedited lead times without violating must-haves; bounded accept waiting and skipped model grace on terminal replies. Model score improved 0.521725 → 0.573210. Final code play obtained EUR 29.50/35 days and 0.676181. The anchor/concession path still fails to secure the historical EUR 28.42 deal. |
| P07 | Correct 24-month coverage/90-day payment, but supplier stopped at EUR 5.46 with the model and EUR 5.40 without it, against historical EUR 5.37. | Retested after lock/guard/no-resend fixes. Final offers were accepted promptly, not countered past withdrawal. Further opening/wording calibration remains unproven; no numerical bug was found that explains the residual price gap. |
| P08 | Supplier insisted on an index clause; wider deadband menus incurred a price premium and quickly reached final. Model EUR 5.67/5% band differs from historical EUR 5.47/5% band. | Added demanded-series/deadband filtering and persistent revealed-price locks. Code obtained EUR 5.49/0% band and 0.393752; model scored 0.332313. This policy change did not close the gap and some experiments worsened the score. |
| P10 | Coverage/must-have repair held, but the supplier immediately made a valid final offer: EUR 31.90 with model, EUR 31.70 without, versus historical EUR 31.60. | Verified full 23,400 annual volume/24 months and immediate final acceptance. No unsafe counter after final was used to chase the score. Opening lead-time/price calibration remains a strategy gap. |
| P18 | Payment/index sequencing left EUR 5.60/0% band with model or EUR 5.80/5% band in code play. Cheaper historical/alternative IDs were refused, then the current offer was accepted. | Retested the deadband/lock changes and robust accept ladder. Best observed score in this work was 0.319096, not 0.453; the wider-band experiment regressed. Payment/deadband premium calibration remains unresolved. |

These causes distinguish observed supplier behaviour from inferred tuning opportunities. A passing
unit test does not prove a negotiation will reach a historical score, and cross-run differences do
not establish that model wording alone caused the difference.

## Timing, claims, and consistency review

All ten model cases ended in deals, all returned `must_haves_ok: true`, and all closed before 420
seconds (maximum 322.0). There were **no contradicted claims** and **no buyer emails missing the
Hollerau company signature** in the corrected simulator, sandbox or hosted evidence. Model writer
calls in the ten-case sweep took at most 11.7 seconds, with no writer errors.

The model P05 sweep, its lead-time retest and the final code-only sweep each contain one structured
timeout on the deliberately idled, uncompetitive Hrvelec thread. An earlier code-only baseline also
timed out a Fuchsreiter reply.
These are not clean passes of the literal every-reply-within-60-seconds acceptance rule. The runner
now polls slow POSTs after 3 seconds, waits for rivals no longer than 45 seconds after its own reply,
and refreshes on refused accepts. The remaining idle-bidder timing policy conflict is explicit.
Hosted records lack per-email delivery timestamps, so absence of timeout records is evidence, not a
proof of an exact maximum end-to-end reply latency.

[DESIGN_NOTES.md](DESIGN_NOTES.md) collects precedence and judgement calls. Important deviations:
whole-cent quantization prevents literal EUR 1 equal-cost precision on large lots; opening-price-only
cost estimates are exempted from the inherited full-cost anchor/floor; and voluntarily idling an RFQ
bidder can conflict with literal universal reply timing. The demanded-index/revealed-price policy
also needs further performance tuning. None is silently counted as full requirement compliance.

No final-wave sessions were started, no unrelated user files were removed, and no commit was made.
The completed artifacts are ready for review, but score/timing acceptance is not yet fully achieved.
# Tacto Negotiation Arena - starter kit

A Python client for the arena API, two example buyer agents that negotiate by e-mail, helpers that
read the suppliers' documents and price a term sheet, a runner that plays many cases in parallel,
`arena-sim` - a local simulator of the arena's API - and a read-only MCP server over the data
package. Read the brief first
(`../brief/brief.md`); the full API is in `../brief/api.md`. Code: MIT.

## Quickstart - first agent on the board in 15 minutes

You need Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

**1. Get your team's key** (one per team): open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a
contact e-mail, and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once an organiser approves,
the key appears **once** on that page - copy it and press "Got the key". Only that page (or its
link) shows it; lost it → ask the organisers to reset it. Keep it out of git.

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv sync --all-extras            # 2. install
cp .env.example .env            # 3. put ARENA_URL and your key (ARENA_API_KEY) into .env
uv run arena me                 # 4. your team and its practice quota
uv run arena cases              # 5. the practice cases (the 10 hosted ones are playable)
uv run arena play case:P01 -v   # 6. the naive agent negotiates one case
uv run arena board              # 7. you are on the practice leaderboard
```

Is the arena up? `curl $ARENA_URL/health`.

Step 6 prints the deal, your total cost `c_deal` against `c_open` and `c_best`, the case score,
and a **replay link**: every e-mail and the supplier's reasons for each move, in words. That is
the learning loop - play a practice case, read the replay, improve your agent, play
again. In practice your best score per case counts, so play a case again whenever your agent improves.
**Quota:** 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours. `arena play` and `arena run` print
how many are left; `arena run` plays only the hosted practice cases and stops starting new ones
once the quota is used up (a `429` there does not go away by retrying). Plan your runs.

**Now the LLM agent.** Download the data (`ARENA_DATA=data/package` in `.env`), choose a model in
`.env` (your own key), then:

```bash
uv run arena data                                          # unpacks data/package (and the Sunday release once public)
uv run arena play case:P01 --agent llm -v
uv run arena run --set practice --agent llm --parallel 8   # every hosted practice case, 8 at a time
uv run arena play case:D02 -v                              # the sandbox: 3 demo suppliers, no board
```

**Sunday 08:00:** run `arena data` again - it adds `data/release-sunday` (new news, letters, a
memo). `DataPackage` merges its facts and documents automatically; hidden cases may cite them.

**Master data file:** convert the downloaded package (and an available Sunday release) into one
`master.json` with:

```bash
uv run arena-build-master-data data/package
```

`DataPackage` reads that JSON for lookups, documents, cases and negotiation dossiers. It refreshes
the file automatically when source files change. Its general `query()` method creates a temporary,
read-only in-memory SQLite view from the JSON rows; it does not reopen the source database.

## Hello World (local, 3 commands)

No key yet? Play a whole case against the local simulator - no network, no quota, no LLM costs.
The simulator's supplier is a plain script; the real ones are on arena.tacto.ai. After
`uv sync --all-extras` (step 2 above):

```bash
# terminal 1: the simulator (--data is optional: leave it out until you have run `arena data`)
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package
# terminal 2: a simulator key, then the naive agent plays case:S01
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Hello World" sim                  # prints an api_key
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 ARENA_API_KEY=<the api_key> uv run arena play case:S01 -v
```

It prints the deal, `c_deal` against `c_open` and `c_best`, the score and a replay link - open it
in your browser: the result on top, then every e-mail of the negotiation.

## SpecAgent requirements and rehearsals

`--agent spec` uses code for prices, term sheets and closing decisions, with the configured model
for supplier profiles, extraction and wording. See [DESIGN_NOTES.md](DESIGN_NOTES.md) for precedence
choices and explicit deviations, and [FINAL_REPORT.md](FINAL_REPORT.md) for tests, scores and remaining
acceptance gaps.

```bash
uv run pytest -q
uv run ruff check arena_kit tests
uv run python -m arena_kit.spec.evaluate --set sandbox --out runs/my-sandbox
uv run python -m arena_kit.spec.evaluate --sim --out runs/my-sim
uv run python -m arena_kit.spec.evaluate --set practice --parallel 5 --out runs/my-practice
```

Each output directory must be new. Evaluations retain exact scores, sessions, threads, model
prompts/replies, source fingerprints and timeout/claim audits. Hosted practice consumes your arena
quota; model-enabled runs send the fictional case material to your configured provider and consume
model credits. Add `--no-model` for the code-only fallback benchmark, or `--ids P05` for a targeted
retest. Do not publish logs if you later use this agent with real confidential business data.

## Try it by hand (Postman, curl)

Feel the API before you put a model in front of it. On the real arena (practice and sandbox) the
60-second rule applies: three late replies in a row end the thread - too fast for typing. **By
hand, use the simulator first**, without the clock:

```bash
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package           # data/package from `arena data`; --data is optional
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Team Name" sim   # prints a simulator api_key
export SIM=http://127.0.0.1:8000 KEY=<the api_key>
```

Every call sends `X-API-Key: <key>`; every `POST` also `Content-Type: application/json` and a
fresh `X-Move-Id` (any unique string - the same id again returns the same answer). In Postman:
those headers, the body as raw JSON.

```bash
# 1. the cases: case:S01 has one supplier, sup:70270, and the negotiable fields unit_price, payment_days
curl -s "$SIM/v1/cases?set=practice" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"

# 2. open a session: the reply carries session_id (sim1 on a fresh simulator) and each supplier's quote e-mail
curl -s -X POST "$SIM/v1/sessions" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Move-Id: open-1" -d '{"case_id": "case:S01"}'

# 3. the supplier's opening e-mail: its term sheet (offer:70270-0) and the quote PDF to fetch
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"

# 4. your e-mail with an offer: the reply is the supplier's answer (status, term_sheets, claim_results)
curl -s -X POST "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270/messages" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Move-Id: msg-1" \
  -d '{"message": {"subject": "Adapter piece HI", "body": "Thank you for your quote. We offer 15.50 EUR at 60 days.",
       "term_sheets": [{"terms": {"unit_price": 15.5, "payment_days": 60}}]}}'

# 5. read the reply in the thread, and the session state
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"
```

To close, send `{"message": {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": "offer:70270-1"}}}` (the
term sheet you take) or `{"message": {"action": {"type": "walk_away"}}}` to the same `messages` path;
the answer carries the result and score. The quote PDF: `GET $SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/attachments/att:70270-0-quote`.
The same calls work on the arena (`https://arena.tacto.ai`, your team's key, a practice case) - with
the clock running.

## The Live Final: waves, in parallel, within the cap

The final comes in 5 themed waves. A wave holds several hidden cases that appear when the host
starts it; play them all in parallel (up to 10 open sessions per key). Each wave has a hard
cap - **8 minutes** (the host may extend one) - and what is still open then ends without a deal.
Start the runner before the first wave and leave it running:

# Tacto Negotiation Arena - Participant brief

> **Build an AI buyer agent that negotiates by e-mail with tough, realistic industrial suppliers,
> gets the best total deal - and can explain how it got there.**

## 1. The story

You are the procurement team of **Hollerau Pumpenwerke GmbH**, a fictional German pump maker:
centrifugal pumps for buildings, water and industry, about €250M revenue, 900 people, one plant in
Bavaria. Your team buys the parts of the pump line - castings, machined parts, sheet metal, seals,
motors, fasteners, stainless bar - from about 45 suppliers. Today is **30 September 2026**, and the
inbox is full: a foundry announces +9.5% on volute casings "due to energy and wages", a framework
contract expires, a new pump series needs three quotes, a supplier with a red scorecard has to fix
its quality.

You answer the way buyers do: by e-mail. On the other side sit our **supplier bots**, each with a
small team of **roles** behind it - the sales rep or owner who writes to you, a boss who must
approve bigger moves, and engineering, quality, logistics, finance or legal, who answer their
topics and attach documents.

Tacto is the AI for industrial procurement: it gives procurement teams the intelligence to source
every part at the best possible terms with minimal effort. Your company runs on that kind of data -
orders, deliveries, invoices, contracts, scorecards, market indices, should-cost estimates, notes
from supplier calls. Your job is to build the agent that turns this data into better deals. (In
Tacto's product, agents such as the Defender Agent or the Sourcing Agent do parts of this job.)

## 2. The task

Each **case** is one negotiation: a trigger (a letter, an expiring contract, an RFQ), your case
file (need, goal, rates, must-haves, your alternative) and one to three supplier bots. Your
**buyer agent**

1. **prepares** - reads the case file and mines the data package;
2. **negotiates by e-mail** - plain-language messages with up to three **term sheets** (alternative
   packages), the data IDs your arguments rest on, and attachments if you like;
3. **closes** - accepts one supplier term sheet, or walks away.

**How a supplier decides.** Each supplier is a company with its own economics and a person at the
desk - a family foundry that remembers how you treated it, a group with an approval ladder, a job
shop that needs cash and work, a near-monopolist that barely moves. Its hard limits come from its
own situation: it never sells below its cost floor, bigger moves need the boss's approval, data
you cite is checked by ID, and it gives nothing without a move from you. Inside those limits it
decides as that person would - reading your whole e-mail: the term sheets, the data, and what you
signal (questions, arguments, threats, appreciation, urgency). It reacts to tone and relationship
as people do; padding does not buy price.

**Data is not automatically rewarded.** True data can disarm a supplier ("we didn't know that") -
or meet "that's not our reality", because something else weighs more for it right now. The traces
are in the data: call notes, letters, news, the remarks on its quotes. The skill is reading the
supplier, not stacking evidence - and finding the trade it wants: a supplier short of cash may care
more about when it is paid than about the price; one that cannot touch its list price may still
move on other terms.

## 3. What you get (Sat 10:00)

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| This brief, the API docs (`api.md`) and the submission guide (`submission.md`) | `https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit`, folder `brief/` |
| **Data package v1**: CSV, the same data as SQLite, `facts.json` (every citable ID with the values the arena checks), contracts, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes - the data behind all 19 practice cases | `https://arena.tacto.ai/v1/data/package.zip`, or the repo's `data/` |
| **Practice arena**: 10 hosted practice cases, picked so every case type shows up; a replay after every case; practice leaderboard; a **sandbox** with 3 demo suppliers | `https://arena.tacto.ai` with your team's key - apply at `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply` (below) |
| **Starter kit**: Python client, a naive agent, an LLM agent that writes e-mails and reads the attached documents, the Live Final runner, an MCP server over the data, `arena-sim` - the API on your laptop | the repo's `starter-kit/` - first agent on the board in 15 minutes |

You bring your own LLM access; we only run the suppliers. Data and docs are CC BY 4.0, code MIT.

**Your key - one per team.** Open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a contact e-mail,
and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once we approve, the key appears **once**
on that page: copy it, press "Got the key". Only that page shows it; lost it - we reset it.
Tip: your team name may start with one emoji - it shows on the big screen (optional; nothing offensive).

**Practice quota: 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours.** `GET /v1/me` shows what
you have used and when it frees up. The build page `https://arena.tacto.ai/live` shows every team's quota use,
practice records and highlights from Sat 10:00 to Sun 12:00.

**`arena-sim`** speaks the arena's API exactly, with one plain scripted supplier: get your plumbing
right there. It teaches the contract, not the suppliers - and we don't hand out our suppliers. Want
a local opponent? Build your own supplier simulator from the public data: thinking into how real
suppliers act is part of the challenge.

**The learning loop:** play a practice case, read your exact score and its cost breakdown, open
the replay - every e-mail and the supplier's reasons in words, as a real supplier would give them -
improve your agent, play again. Your best score per practice case counts.

## 4. The data

The buyer's world: supplier and part master data; three years of orders, goods receipts,
invoices and payments; quality notifications and quarterly scorecards (on-time delivery, PPM);
framework contracts and clauses; past RFQs and quotes; forecasts; supplier intel and news; past
negotiations, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes; should-cost estimates; spend down to the
long tail; and monthly market indices (real public series, frozen at 2026-09-30).

- **Every fact you can cite has an ID** `<type>:<id>[@period]`, e.g. `po:4500010001-10`,
  `idx:PPI-C2451@2026-08`, `sc:70110@2026Q3`, `ctr:4600070110#3.1`, `doc:…`.
- What moves a supplier is in the data - some of it only in the notes and e-mails. Some notes are
  just noise. The company and its suppliers are fictional.
- **Sunday 08:00: a second release** - market news, supplier letters and a memo from early October
  (`GET /v1/data` lists it). Hidden cases may cite its facts. Your agent should read it.

## 5. How a negotiation works

- **Round 0:** every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once, with a quote PDF.
- **Your message:** subject, body, up to 3 term sheets (each with a value for every negotiable
  field), the data IDs you rely on (IDs written in the body count too), optional text attachments.
- **The supplier answers by e-mail:** the role in charge writes; its standing term sheet; a status -
  `open`, `final_offer` (push further and it may walk), `agreed` (it offers exactly your terms; you
  still accept), `walked_away`, `no_bid`; signals (reply delay, quote validity); fields it left out;
  and how each data argument checked out. A supplier's reply can take **up to about a minute**;
  its time never counts against your 60 seconds.
- **Only you close a deal**, by accepting a supplier's standing term sheet. In **RFQ cases** 2-3
  suppliers run in parallel threads; accepting one ends the case.
- **Limits:** a round limit per thread (default 10 messages) and **60 seconds per message**, counted
  from the supplier's reply. A late message counts as
  a timeout: your last offer repeated, the supplier's patience drops; three in a row, or one after
  the last round, end the thread.
- **Unstated terms default to the supplier's standard terms** - listed in its quote PDF.

**Documents** are rendered from the supplier's data, never invented: the quote PDF (read it before
you accept), a cost breakdown XLSX (ask; an open supplier sends one), an 8D report (quality), a
delivery schedule XLSX (logistics), and the order confirmation at the deal.

**What counts:** **term sheets bind** - nothing else. **Data you cite is checked**: the reply says
`verified`, `contradicted` (a wrong figure or an unknown ID - it costs trust), `irrelevant` or
`duplicate`; whether a true argument moves the supplier, and how far, is the supplier's business.
**What you write is understood** - and has consequences, as it would with a person.

## 6. The score: total cost in €

Only the accepted term sheet scores. The case values it as the **total cost C** of covering your
**fixed need over a fixed horizon**, at the case's published rates. Every case states its
**category goal** - `stabilise`, `secure_supply`, `quality_first`, `leverage` or `routine` - and its
rates follow it. Reaching the goal is the skill.

| Part of C | How |
|---|---|
| Price | committed units × unit price; units bought before a new price takes effect at the current price |
| Uncovered need | need the deal does not cover at the fallback price, plus the goal's fallback risk on it |
| Payment, freight, lead time | interest for paying earlier than your reference; freight by Incoterm; € per day beyond your need |
| Quality, other | expected defects at the committed PPM minus chargebacks; tooling; an index clause on the case's index path, plus the goal's index risk |
| The supplier's health | strategic and bottleneck goals only: € for every margin point the deal leaves the supplier below a sustainable margin (its margin on the cash it gets) |

**Case score = (C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best)**, clipped to 0…1. **C_open** is the best
opening quote. **C_best** is the cheaper of the best package any supplier in the case would ever
accept, with every valid lever applied, and your alternative - fixed per case, so good arguments
raise your score instead of moving the yardstick. **No deal** scores your alternative (0 if none);
some cases are best left without a deal. **A broken must-have** scores 0. **In the final** each
wave scores 0-100 (the mean of its case scores × 100, one decimal) and your **points so far** are the
sum of your wave scores - up to 500 after five waves. The formula is in `api.md`; `arena_kit.total_cost` computes C.

**Example** (a `leverage` case: 3 % fallback risk) - need 4,000 a year for 2 years, interest 8%,
reference 60 days. The foundry asks €43.20 for a 24-month contract at 30 days net.

| | Terms | C |
|---|---|---|
| C_open | €43.20, 30 days: 8,000 × 43.20 = 345,600, plus 30 days of early payment at 8% = 2,304 | €347,904 |
| Your deal | €41.60, 60 days: 8,000 × 41.60 = 332,800 | €332,800 |
| C_best (hidden) | €40.80, 90 days: 326,400, minus 30 days of interest saved = 2,176 | €324,224 |
| **Score** | (347,904 − 332,800) / (347,904 − 324,224) | **0.64** |

The same €41.60 for 12 months covers half your need; the rest counts at the fallback price, say
€46.00, plus 3 %: C = €355,920 - worse than the opening, score 0.

## 7. Rules

1. **Not allowed:** humans in the loop during the Live Final, attacks on the service or on other
   teams, more than one API key per team - and agents that read the live feed during the Live
   Final: the event feed, the screen and the leaderboard (`/v1/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard`
   and their JSON).
2. **Everything else counts** - including weaknesses you find in our bots. Replays show how every
   score came about, and the jury may weigh that in the pitches. The goal is to convince a
   realistic supplier: that is what carries over to real negotiations.
3. **One attempt per case** in the final. An abandoned case is no deal.
4. **Code freeze at Sun 12:00.** Submit on ehl.gg: your repo (the agent and a README to run it), the
   commit hash, a short description and your pitch slides (`submission.md`). The final runs that
   commit, so your agent must be running and polling before 12:00. We check the top 10 for later
   pushes. Run your agent where you like, with your own LLM keys.
5. A supplier remembers only within a case; its history with your company is in the data.

## 8. The weekend

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Sat 10:00 | Kickoff and reveal: brief, data, kit, practice arena live |
| Sat 12:00-13:00 | Deep dive (ground floor, room on the signs): data, API, kit, Q&A - challenge selection closes 13:00 |
| Sat afternoon | Office hours at the Tacto table; practice all weekend |
| Sat ⟦TIME⟧ | Tacto stops answering for the night (Discord: https://discord.gg/hPwFfbWRV) |
| Sun 08:00 | **Sunday release:** new market news and letters (`/v1/data`) |
| Sun 09:00 | **Pre-flight:** one practice case through your final setup |
| Sun 12:00-~12:58 | **Code + slides freeze**, then the **Live Final** in 5 waves |
| Sun 13:00-14:30 | Top 10 pitch to the Tacto jury (5 min pitch + 2 min questions) |
| Sun 14:30 | Track winners and the two finalists announced |
| Sun 15:30 | Grand Final pitches (AudiMax) |
| Sun 16:30 | Awards |

**The Live Final.** The hidden cases come in **5 themed waves**. The host shows each wave's
theme on the big screen, then starts the wave; its cases appear at the start, for all teams at once,
each in its own order, one session per case. **Each wave has a hard cap of 8 minutes:** threads
still open at the cap end with no deal (your alternative's score). Start your agent before the
first wave and keep it running: it plays all of a wave's cases **in parallel** (up to 10 open
sessions per key) - the kit's `arena run --set final` does that. The leaderboard shows your points
so far, wave by wave; replays and the suppliers' back office appear after the final. A case broken on our side is replayed.

The hidden cases share the world, case types and rules of the practice set, with new suppliers and
settings. **Up to a third of them combine supplier types and case types that practice never shows**
- no new rules, but an agent that memorised the practice suppliers will meet strangers. Some cite
the Sunday release.

## 9. Selection and prizes

- **Top 10:** the 10 teams with the most points after the five waves pitch to our jury from 13:00:
  5 minutes + 2 minutes of questions. Every replay is open to the jury.
- **Track places 1-3** (open to all teams of the track): ⟦PLACEHOLDER - decided Sat morning:
  weighting of Live Final score vs. jury score, and the jury criteria (draft: approach,
  explainability, craft)⟧.
- **EHL Grand Final:** the best 2 of the 5 EHL finalist teams in this track go on to the Grand Final
  pitches. Finalist teams outside the top 10 are ranked by the Live Final score alone.
- **Ties:** points are points; an exact tie goes to more deals, then fewer rounds. At the top-10
  cut the jury looks at the score distribution. **Prizes:** €1,500 for 1st place, medals for the
  top 3, handed over by Tacto at the awards at 16:30.

## 10. Tips

- **Numbers come from code, the model writes.** Compute C for every term sheet; put figures from
  the data next to their IDs; let the LLM choose arguments and wording.
- **Read the supplier** before you argue: its notes, letters, news and quote remarks tell you what
  it is dealing with - and what will move it.
- **Read the quote PDF** before you accept: what you did not negotiate closes on its standard terms.
- **Ask, and offer alternatives.** Two or three term sheets show you what a supplier values.
- **Don't leak** urgency, a budget or a missing alternative. Don't take the first offer.
- **Plan your practice runs** (200 a day is for learning, not brute force) and **rehearse the
  final**: all hosted cases in parallel, from Sunday's machine and network, well inside 8 minutes.

129	### 0.6 The opening quotes and the replies
130	
131	`POST /v1/sessions` also returns `opening`, one entry per supplier:
132	
133	```json
134	"sup:70240": {"offer_id": "offer:70240-0", "round": 0, "status": "open",
135	              "terms": {"unit_price": 31.5, "lead_time_days": 52},
136	              "alternatives": [],
137	              "missing_fields": ["payment_days"],
138	              "claims": [], "claim_results": [],
139	              "signals": {"reply_delay_days": 4, "validity_days": 30},
140	              "text": "Hello, Thank you for your enquiry. ..."}
141	```
142	
143	- **`terms` can be partial.** Fields in `missing_fields` close on the supplier's **standard terms**
144	  (in the quote PDF) - fill them from the PDF before computing C; never assume our reference values.
145	- **An opening quote can break a must-have** (P05: 52 days against `<= 42`) - repair it (R11.9).
146	- `alternatives`: `[{offer_id, terms}]` - extra packages, acceptable like the main sheet (R12.11).
147	- Replies (`POST …/messages`) carry `status` (`open`, `final_offer`, `agreed`, `walked_away`,
148	  `no_bid`), `term_sheets` (its standing offer, `offer:` ID), `claim_results` per argument,
149	  `signals`, `missing_fields` and `attachments` (cost breakdown XLSX, 8D PDF, delivery schedule).

151	### 0.7 What to compute from the case JSON before the first message
152	
153	1. Validate: every `negotiable` field except `unit_price` has `term_options`; no field is both
154	   fixed and negotiable; must-haves name real fields.
155	2. C(terms) with `arena_kit.total_cost`, the opening C of every supplier (standard terms filled),
156	   and C_alt from `buyer.alternative`.
157	3. Coverage: does `contract_months` × `volume_per_year` cover `need_per_year` × `horizon_years`?
158	   If an option closes the gap and lowers C, it goes into message 1 (R12.1-R12.2).
159	4. The lever table (R12.3) over `term_options`, the playbook row for `category_goal` (R13.10), the
160	   anchor (R4, R13.12) and the floor (R2.1, R6.5).
161	5. The must-have filter every sheet and every accept passes through.
162	6. The clock: `round_limit` and, in the final, `seconds_left`.

244	## 1. Prepare before the clock
245	
246	- **R1.1 Supplier dossier.** Before the session's first move, gather for every supplier everything
247	  in the data package: call and meeting notes, letters, past negotiations (asked vs settled), its
248	  financials, our payment record, scorecards, should-cost, the part's cost drivers and contract
249	  clauses (`dossier.gather`, Sunday release included). Cache it per supplier and parts.
250	- **R1.2 Cash signals.** Scan the dossier for cash-pressure words (cash, liquidity, skonto, prepay,
251	  credit line, working capital, insolvency, short-time work, "within N days") and record the hits.
252	- **R1.3 One profile call per supplier, in parallel.** A model reads the dossier plus the computed
253	  data arguments and returns JSON only:
254	  `persona, tone, pressures[], wants[], levers[], avoid[], cash_short, claim_ranking[], questions[], angle`.
255	  Timeout 90 s for all profiles together.
256	- **R1.4 Validate the profile.** `levers` are mapped onto the case's negotiable field names and
257	  `claim_ranking` onto real argument keys; anything that does not match is dropped. `cash_short` is
258	  true if the model says so, or if the dossier has cash signals and payment_days is the top lever.
259	- **R1.5 Default profile.** If the call fails or times out, use a default profile: polite, factual,
260	  constructive tone; levers = payment_days first when cash signals exist, then the case type's levers
261	  (`TYPE_LEVERS` below). A missing profile never costs the case.
262	
263	`TYPE_LEVERS`: price_increase → effective_date, payment_days · raw_material → index_clause,
264	payment_days, contract_months · renewal → contract_months, volume_per_year, payment_days · bundling →
265	contract_months, payment_days · capacity → volume_per_year, lead_time_days, contract_months ·
266	quality → chargeback_eur_per_complaint, ppm_commitment · rfq → payment_days, lead_time_days, tooling_eur.
267	
268	## 2. Our estimate of the supplier
269	
270	- **R2.1 Full cost, calibrated.** In this order: the supplier's own cost-breakdown XLSX (sum of EUR
271	  elements, without margin and totals); else should-cost / 1.02 (fits the arena's relationship charge
272	  over 31 recorded deals - `FULL_COST_K` in `team/agent.py` and the current MESO agent); else opening
273	  price / 1.10. Not too high: a high floor made BuyerAgent stop pushing (P01, 10 Oct: accepted 136.30
274	  where 133.70 was reachable). Not too low either: with its "low end of the confidence band"
275	  estimate BuyerAgent saw no cost in squeezing P02's supplier to EUR 351 - the arena charged EUR
276	  124,110 for it (score 0.211; DualAgent 0.385 at EUR 373).
277	- **R2.2 Cost of money.** The buyer's interest rate, plus 6 points for a supplier short of cash.
278	  Once the supplier has priced payment days itself (two of its sheets differ only in payment), use
279	  that revealed rate instead (slope × 360, clamped to 3-40 %) - see R12.4.
280	- **R2.3 Margin charge only where the goal has one.** C includes the supplier's margin penalty only
281	  for stabilise and secure_supply.
282	
283	## 3. What we negotiate on
284	
285	- **R3.1 Best sheet on the table.** For each thread, take the supplier's cheapest offer for us among
286	  its standing sheet *and* its alternatives, preferring ones that keep the must-haves.
287	- **R3.2 Both-sides-gain structure (`mutual_combo`).** Move each of the supplier's non-price terms
288	  toward what the supplier prefers for as long as that also lowers our C (e.g. a longer contract that
289	  covers our whole need). The price is negotiated on this structure, not on the quote as sent.
290	- **R3.3 Asks are never free (`reference_combo`).** Terms the supplier pulled beyond our reference
291	  (payment days, volume, contract length, lead time, no index clause) are put back where that saves
292	  us money before pricing the target - what it asks for is paid for in price.
293	
294	## 4. The opening anchor
295	
296	- **R4.1 Anchor from the data.** The lowest of: the goal's cut off the best quote (leverage 12 %,
297	  routine 8 %, quality_first 6 %, stabilise 6 %, secure_supply 5 %); the current price (no increase
298	  at all) for price_increase and raw_material cases; the fair price = should-cost / (1 − margin)
299	  (leverage 5 %, routine 6 %, quality_first 8 %; the sustainable margin for relationship goals).
300	- **R4.2 Credibility limits.** Never more than 25 % under the supplier's price; never under its
301	  estimated full cost × 1.01; never under the price at which C stops falling.
302	- **R4.3 RFQ.** Every bidder is anchored to the best quote in the case, not its own (D02: anchored
303	  to its own 17.10, the dearer bidder agreed to 15.09 at once; about 13 was reachable).
304	- **R4.4 Fixed anchor.** The anchor is set once per thread.
305	
306	## 5. Concessions: reciprocal, never stuck
307	
308	- **R5.1 Curve.** Our k-th offer closes `1 − (1 − k/H)^1.6` of the gap from the anchor to the
309	  supplier's C; H = 6 (5 in an RFQ). Steps shrink over time.
310	- **R5.2 Reciprocity.** Track the supplier's C after every reply (one entry per reply, so a hold shows
311	  as a zero step). If it moved more than 0.1 % of C: our step = max(min(planned, 0.5 × its step),
312	  0.4 % of C). We move by less than it did, but always visibly.
313	- **R5.3 Deadlock breaker (the key difference from DualAgent).** If the supplier did not move, hold
314	  **once**; the next round make one real step to break the deadlock: at least 15 % of the C gap left
315	  (TeamAgent's measure, R12.5), and never less than 0.4 % of C. Never stall two rounds, never close
316	  just because both sides held. Never a token step (D01: "a nominal adjustment of one cent" was
317	  called out).
318	- **R5.4 Still moving means ask again.** If the supplier's offer meets our target but it is still
319	  conceding (> 0.4 % of C last round) and more than 3 rounds are left, set the target to
320	  `their C − 0.5 × their last step` and keep negotiating.
321	- **R5.5 Caps.** The target never exceeds 0.995 × the alternative's C. In an RFQ it is at most 0.99 ×
322	  the best rival's C, and never below the anchor.
323	
324	## 6. Term sheets
325	
326	- **R6.1 Up to three sheets, all at the target C** (`strategy.sheets`): our terms (every term at its
327	  best for us, at a higher price), their terms (the both-sides-gain structure), and a give (one lever
328	  from the profile moved toward the supplier, for a lower price). "Our terms" goes first.
329	- **R6.2 Shared surplus on a give.** When a term is worth more to the supplier than it costs us (e.g.
330	  faster payment to a cash-short supplier), price the give halfway between our equal-cost price and the
331	  supplier's indifference price (`give_price`, `SURPLUS_SHARE = 0.5`). Both sides are better off
332	  taking it.
333	- **R6.3 The supplier asked for something.** Send two sheets instead: exactly its ask at a lower
334	  price (shared surplus), and our reference terms at the target price. No third sheet that blurs the
335	  trade (`ask_sheets`).
336	- **R6.4 Decoy.** Arrange the sheets as lean / recommended / other. The lean one is the recommended
337	  sheet 2 % cheaper with the supplier's most-valued term moved our way, so the middle one looks
338	  sensible. It is safe: if the supplier takes the lean one, that is better for us (`with_decoy`).
339	- **R6.5 Sheet floor.** No sheet below max(estimated full cost × 0.97, 75 % of the supplier's price).
340	  P18, 10 Oct: a give at 28 % under was not credible and the supplier did not move.
341	- **R6.6 Out of reach.** If no sheet fits the target, send the supplier's own terms at
342	  max(floor, 99 % of its price), provided the must-haves hold.
343	- **R6.7 Every sheet keeps the must-haves** and is cheaper than what the supplier asks.
344	
345	## 7. When to close
346	
347	Accept the cheapest standing sheet that keeps the must-haves and beats the alternative when:
348	
349	- **R7.1** the supplier agreed to our terms;
350	- **R7.2** it made a final offer (single thread; in an RFQ only if every thread is final or this is
351	  the best offer on the table);
352	- **R7.3** its offer meets our next target - unless it is still moving with more than 3 rounds left
353	  (R5.4);
354	- **R7.4** its offer is as good as what we last offered;
355	- **R7.5** at most one round is left in the thread (or in every RFQ thread);
356	- **R7.6** the planned rounds are over (H + 2 offers in every thread).
357	
358	Walk away only when nothing on the table is acceptable and every thread is at a final offer or out of
359	rounds. **No** deadlock close and **no** walk-risk close: those ended DualAgent's P11 and P18 early.

369	## 9. The e-mail
370	
371	- **R9.1 The model writes words only** (the kit's `writing.SYSTEM` JSON parts: salutation, opening,
372	  argument keys, bridge, question, closing). Code inserts the arguments word for word and the options
373	  paragraph from the term sheets, then lints (no leaks, no figures that are not in the material, no
374	  unknown IDs).
375	- **R9.2 What the writer sees:** the supplier's profile (persona, tone, pressures, wants, avoid,
376	  angle); its last e-mail with sender, status, subject and non-quote attachments; how our arguments
377	  have checked out so far; our last two e-mails; how far it moved toward us in % since our last
378	  e-mail; the options; up to 6 arguments ranked by the profile's `claim_ranking`; the questions.
379	- **R9.3 Plain stance per move** (`_stance`):
380	  - first e-mail: "We open: our options are ambitious; give the reasons, not apologies."
381	  - hold while they are still coming down: acknowledge the step briefly, say the price is still too
382	    high and why;
383	  - hold because they did not move: polite but firm, do not thank them for flexibility they did not
384	    show, give one concrete reason or ask what would let them move;
385	  - step: "a modest step - this costs us and we expect a step back."
386	- **R9.4 Questions.** One per e-mail at most, never repeated: a cost breakdown once (unless already
387	  asked or received - an open supplier sends one, and R2.1 uses it), then the case type's question
388	  (8D report, delivery schedule, shortest lead time, which cost elements rose, which volume or term
389	  would improve the price, bundle parts, fair base month and deadband), then the profile's questions.
390	- **R9.5 Arguments.** From `claims.candidates` (code-computed, checked IDs). Each ID once per case;
391	  an argument that came back `contradicted` is never used again; news the profile ranks as helpful
392	  counts as favourable. Even a fallback e-mail carries the two best arguments.
393	- **R9.6 Company name** from the data, else from the supplier's subject ("Quote from X:") or
394	  signature - never the bare supplier ID (D02: "Dear colleagues at sup:DEMO-J1").
395	- **R9.7 Allowed figures** come only from the supplier's e-mails, the trigger letter, the contract
396	  clauses, our arguments and the options paragraph.

491	## 12. From TeamAgent
492	
493	### 12.1 Message 1 carries the deal
494	
495	- **R12.1 Put the whole structure into the first message.** Mined from ~80 recorded practice
496	  negotiations (`AGENTS.md`): the supplier's reply to our first message gained +0.46 score on
497	  average, replies 2-4 together +0.08. The first message already carries full coverage (R12.2), the
498	  payment variants, the rival's offer (RFQ) and the strongest arguments. Every best TeamAgent run
499	  (P04, P05, P07, P08, P10) did this.
500	- **R12.2 Coverage lock.** Commit the full need for the full horizon from message 1 whenever the
501	  lever table says covering it lowers C (P08: 24 months on a 2-year need; 12-month packages scored
502	  0.08 vs 0.44 there; P10: the volume was cut below the must-have in 4/4 runs without it). Once our
503	  sheet A covers the need, no sheet we send covers less - not even one the model writes. Trust the
504	  table when coverage does **not** pay: P08's fallback EUR 5.72 was below the offer's 5.98.
505	
506	### 12.2 Levers priced in euros
507	
508	- **R12.3 Lever table** (`team/levers.py`). For the supplier's standing sheet, move every negotiable
509	  field to each allowed option, and the price by 1 %; the change in C is the lever's value in EUR and
510	  in EUR per unit (`price_equiv`). Ask only for levers worth at least 0.3 % of C (coverage always
511	  counts): suppliers price every demand in, at 3-7× its value for faster lead time or chargebacks -
512	  ask only what the need requires.
513	- **R12.4 Revealed lever prices.** When two of the supplier's sheets (main and alternative) differ in
514	  one term, that pair is its own price for the term (`revealed_slopes`). With it, a lever counts only
515	  if it saves us more than the supplier charges for it; on a tie (within EUR 1) take the option closest
516	  to the supplier's own value - no stricter ask than needed. Its payment slope is its cost of money
517	  (R2.2).
518	
519	### 12.3 Anchor and steps
520	
521	- **R12.5 Steps in C, at least 15 % of the gap.** Mined: messages without a step drew a final offer
522	  37 % of the time, steps of at least 15 % of the gap 17 %. TeamAgent's path gives 0 / 15 / 30 / 45 /
523	  60 % of the gap from anchor to the supplier's C by our 1st ... 5th message, never less than 15 % of
524	  what was left after our last message, and never above 0.997 × the supplier's C. In this agent the
525	  15 % is the size of the deadlock-breaking step (R5.3) and the floor of a step we choose to make;
526	  the reciprocity cap (R5.2) still limits our step when the supplier moved less.
527	- **R12.6 RFQ anchor only falls.** The anchor is the lowest price anyone has put on the table in the
528	  case, cut by the goal's share plus 4 points for competition; in an RFQ it may move down when a
529	  rival goes lower, never up (R4.4 otherwise).
530	
531	### 12.4 Sheets
532	
533	- **R12.7 Payment probe.** One sheet of the first menu varies payment days (to the supplier's own
534	  value, or to 30 days) at equal C: its pick reveals its cost of money (P05: 90/60/30 sheets; the
535	  bidder came back at 30 days and EUR 28.42).
536	- **R12.8 Index clause on the supplier's terms.** When the supplier insists on an index clause, offer
537	  its own series with the deadband that costs us least, never a 0 % deadband we can avoid (P08: its
538	  0 % became 5 % in the final offer).
539	- **R12.9 A floor per structure.** Each variant has its own price floor - faster payment is worth
540	  more to the supplier, so that sheet may go lower. A give worth more than the price room (e.g. half
541	  the need uncovered) is no offer.
542	- **R12.10 Never regress.** Never send a sheet that costs us as much as one the supplier has already
543	  offered (within 0.1 %). If nothing cheaper is left: offer back its earlier, cheaper sheet once, else
544	  accept.

546	### 12.5 Closing
547	
548	- **R12.11 Accept ladder.** Accept from every sheet the supplier ever offered in every live thread -
549	  main sheets and alternatives - cheapest valid first; up to three earlier IDs (cheaper by 0.1 %+)
550	  before the latest ones; a refused accept changes nothing, try the next. Mined: the cheapest sheet
551	  ever offered was often not the one taken (P01 7/7 runs: 0.586 vs 0.550); 30 % of replies carry an
552	  alternative, 38 % of those are cheaper for us than the main sheet.
553	- **R12.12 A final offer is accepted at once.** Any message after a `final_offer` → walked away 8/8;
554	  accepting it → deal 38/38. Only when nothing on the table is acceptable (it breaks a must-have or
555	  loses to our alternative) send **one** repair message: its price, accepted, with the nearest
556	  must-have-keeping option and full coverage (`confirm_final`).
557	- **R12.13 `agreed` or stalled → its earlier cheaper sheet, once.** `agreed` only echoes our last
558	  sheet: if one of its earlier sheets costs us 0.3 % less, offer exactly those terms back first.
559	  Stalled = no cheaper offer over its last three replies after 3+ of our messages.

634	### 13.2 Correct numbers
635	
636	- **R13.8 Solve the price exactly.** Every package is priced so its C equals the target, not by a
637	  rule of thumb:
638	  - without the supplier's margin charge C is linear in the price: `p = (target − C(0)) / (C(1) − C(0))`;
639	  - with it, C is convex in the price: find the cheapest price by golden-section search between 0.5×
640	    and 1.5× the supplier's price, and solve for the target by bisection on the side **above** it
641	    (a price below the cheapest one costs more and leaves the supplier weaker).
642	  Tests: each sheet of a step has the same C within EUR 1.
643	- **R13.9 Data arguments computed the way the arena checks them** (`claims.py`): an index change uses
644	  two months of one series at most 12 months apart, ending within the last 12 months of the data
645	  (frozen at 2026-09); figures rounded as the sentence states them, next to their IDs. Only arguments
646	  that argue our side are offered: an index that **rose** confirms the supplier's case and is kept out
647	  unless it rose less than half the increase asked for (P02, P04). Kinds: index changes, the weighted
648	  summary of the part's own cost drivers ("explain about +x %, not y %", no ID), a letter giving less
649	  notice than the contract requires, scorecard quality and delivery, rival quotes and offers,
650	  should-cost, forecast volume. Each ID once per case; a rival's offer once per supplier.
